title: The Anthropic Prospectus Arrives: My (but not the) IPO valuation!
gist: Damodaran reads Anthropic's 416-page S-1 (filed Oct 26, 2026) and values the equity at ~$1.475 trillion, just below the $1.5-2 trillion offer range, on a story of ~$1 trillion revenue by 2036, a 27.5% target margin (32.5% less 5 points of regulatory drag), $3 of revenue per $1 of capital and a 9.74% cost of capital; his scenario range runs from -$373 billion to $4.04 trillion. He flags that $600B+ of compute commitments have converted the biggest cost from variable to fixed (high operating leverage, BB+ rating), calls the five-share-class plus public-benefit-corporation governance worse than Alphabet/Meta, and says he will sit out (not short) an IPO priced well above value while expecting a later Facebook-2012-style buying opportunity.

insights.claim: Anthropic's S-1 shows revenues in the first two quarters of 2026 about fourteen times those of the first two quarters of 2025, but revenue growth slowed in Q3 2026 as OpenAI regained market share, compute capacity became a constraint and some enterprises moved to cheaper open-source models.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Decelerating growth at IPO undermines run-rate based pricing; watch quarterly sequential growth and share data versus OpenAI post-listing.

insights.claim: Enterprises spending more than $1 million a year on Claude rose to 1,900 from fewer than 100 a year earlier, yet Anthropic's top five customers still account for 25% of revenues.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Customer concentration is a key tail risk; loss or renegotiation by a single large (likely AI-ecosystem) customer would hit revenue materially.

insights.claim: Almost 80% of Anthropic's current revenue comes from enterprises paying based on usage, which Damodaran reads as evidence the company is targeting the premium segment of the AI market.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Usage-based enterprise revenue ties Anthropic's top line to customer activity levels, making it more economically cyclical than seat-based SaaS.

insights.claim: Anthropic's deep operating and financing interconnections with other big AI players (the 'circularity' critics note) create potential for double counting and opacity in its reported revenues.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Discount revenue sourced from investors/partners in the AI stack; scrutinize related-party revenue disclosures.
insights.locator: If I were to summarize the information

insights.claim: Anthropic reported an $80 billion loss for the first half of 2026, but $72 billion of that was a non-cash charge for expensing the conversion option on a convertible bond, leaving an adjusted operating loss of over $8 billion.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Headline GAAP losses are dominated by a one-off derivative charge; screen-based investors reading headline losses will misprice the underlying economics.
insights.quote: The actual loss reported was $80 billion, but $72 billion represented a non-cash charge, expensing the conversion option of the convertible bond.

insights.claim: Anthropic claims an operating profit in its most recent quarter, and all expense categories are falling as a percent of revenue; compute costs, its largest expense, fell from more than 250% of quarterly revenue to 48%.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Rapid operating leverage is real, but one profitable quarter is not a trend; track whether compute/revenue keeps falling as committed capacity hits the P&L.

insights.claim: Anthropic's high reported gross margins are largely an artifact of its huge compute commitments, which moved its biggest expense from variable to fixed cost, raising operating leverage and locking in future recommitments as compute must be replenished.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Gross margin is flattered by contract structure; a revenue shortfall would compress margins sharply because the compute cost base does not flex down.

insights.claim: Despite one quarter of reported profit, Anthropic will need significant continued revenue growth to stay ahead of the expenses from compute commitments that will hit its income statement in future periods.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Anthropic is a growth-dependent survival story; any growth stall turns committed costs into a margin and solvency problem.
insights.locator: The expenses for Anthropic, across categories

themes.theme: Compute commitments as hidden capital and leverage

insights.claim: Anthropic's financial statements do not show its compute investment in capex or balance-sheet debt; instead it discloses hundreds of billions (over $600 billion) of future compute commitments, which Damodaran capitalizes as debt in his valuation.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Off-balance-sheet compute commitments should be treated as lease-like debt when comparing AI labs' leverage and invested capital.

insights.claim: Anthropic is catching up with OpenAI's lead in compute power, but the catch-up has come at a steep cost in future cost commitments.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The compute arms race between frontier labs transfers value to chip and data-center suppliers while loading labs with fixed obligations.

insights.claim: Compute investments, especially chips, age quickly and must be replaced; chip costs may fall, but new models demanding proportionately more power plus data center real estate and power costs (and community opposition to data centers) may more than offset that.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: AI lab reinvestment needs are recurring, not one-off; bullish on long-run demand for chips and power, bearish on lab free cash flow.

insights.claim: Damodaran assumes the compute crunch persists near term but eases over time, so Anthropic needs about $1 of reinvestment for every $3 of additional revenue, in line with current tech-company sales-to-invested-capital, which still implies very large annual dollar reinvestment given the revenue leap.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Sales-to-capital is a major swing factor: at 1x (scarce compute) the equity can be worthless, at 4x it can be worth $4 trillion.

insights.claim: Anthropic's compute, purchase and lease commitments of hundreds of billions expose it to default risk, reflected in a BB+ bond rating, but its $114 billion cash balance plus roughly $100 billion in expected IPO proceeds should cover commitments for the next few years.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Near-term credit risk is buffered by cash; Anthropic credit becomes vulnerable only if growth stalls and the market cap collapses, closing capital access.

insights.claim: Damodaran frames the total AI products and services market around four questions: productivity tool vs employee replacement, top-quintile vs across-the-board wage displacement, few vs most industries, and US-centric vs global reach.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Use these four axes to bound TAM assumptions embedded in any AI-lab valuation.

insights.claim: Damodaran believes AI's most powerful, highest-priced models will displace highly paid white-collar employees in some industries, yielding an end market of $5 trillion or more, with Anthropic positioned as a leader in the premium portion.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: A white-collar-replacement thesis supports premium-model pricing power but is a headwind for labor-intensive professional services businesses.

insights.claim: Damodaran thinks it plausible that Anthropic's revenues approach $1 trillion by 2036, when no company today has over $1 trillion in revenue and Amazon and Walmart sit around $700-750 billion.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Even a bullish-but-valuation-disciplined analyst needs a larger-than-Amazon revenue base to justify the IPO range.

insights.claim: Anthropic's prospectus makes explicit an ambition to compete in businesses its agents disrupt, with pharmaceuticals emerging as a play in which it would use its agents for drug research and testing and capture a portion of revenues from drugs developed.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: AI labs moving downstream threatens drug research and testing service providers (CROs) and could add revenue optionality beyond model sales.

insights.claim: Damodaran expects the mature AI market to split into a mass-market segment of often open-source, less powerful models competing on price with business-services-like operating margins (~10%), and a premium segment of closed frontier models powered by client data with enterprise-software-like margins (~40% for the top quartile).
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Position in the premium vs commodity tier, not scale alone, determines long-run AI margins; commoditized model providers should be valued like services firms.

insights.claim: Assuming a 75% premium / 25% mass-market revenue mix, Damodaran derives a 32.5% pre-tax operating margin for Anthropic, which would rank in the ninth decile of US companies in 2026.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Margin target is aggressive but not extreme; bulls pushing to 40% are assuming a near-pure premium mix.

insights.claim: Damodaran expects AI regulation to arrive (Anthropic and OpenAI have invited it, cynically perhaps to keep out competition, especially from China), and, as with social media, to raise operating costs rather than stop the business, cutting Anthropic's target margin by 5 points from 32.5% to 27.5%.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Regulation is a margin tax not an existential threat; incumbents lobbying for rules may gain a competitive moat versus Chinese and open-source entrants.

insights.claim: Damodaran values Anthropic's equity at $1.475 trillion, at the lower end of the $1.5-2 trillion offer pricing range, using $1 trillion 2036 revenue, 27.5% target margin, sales-to-capital of 3 and a 9.74% cost of capital, with debt including the present value of compute commitments and cash including ~$100 billion of IPO proceeds.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Even an upbeat intrinsic story does not clear the top of the offer range; anything priced well above ~$1.5 trillion is momentum, not value.
insights.quote: With my upbeat story for Anthropic, I estimate a value for the equity of $1.475 trillion, at the lower end of the offer pricing range ($1.5 to $2 trillion).

insights.claim: In Damodaran's worst case ($200 billion 2036 revenue, 10% margins, sales-to-capital of 1, 9.88% cost of capital, drastic regulation) Anthropic's equity is worth -$373 billion and the company would not survive; in the best case ($1.5 trillion revenue, 40% margins, sales-to-capital of 4, 7.79% cost of capital, no regulation) equity is worth $4.04 trillion.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The extreme valuation dispersion (negative to $4 trillion) makes Anthropic a binary-ish story stock; position sizing should reflect that.

insights.claim: Damodaran sets Anthropic's cost of capital at 9.74%, versus a 9.16% median and 9.88% third quartile for US firms in September 2026, and argues it is among the least critical inputs, constrained by what the market offers.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Debates over discount rates are a distraction; revenue scale, margins and reinvestment efficiency drive the value.

insights.claim: Damodaran assigns Anthropic a 10% probability of failure with a loss of half its value in that event, arguing failure risk is suppressed by its cash and capital-market access but both buffers dissipate if revenue growth is anemic.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Distress risk is reflexive with the stock price: a falling market cap removes the capital access that suppresses default risk.

insights.claim: Whether enterprise AI agent spending is sticky is untested; it may prove cyclical, with customers using AI as a productivity tool or employee replacement cutting back or slowing usage in bad economic times.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: A recession would be the first real test of AI revenue stickiness; usage-priced labs are exposed to downturns.

insights.claim: Damodaran argues the S-1 is overanalyzed: it is a snapshot of a young evolving company, akin to judging a kindergartner's report card to fund college, and both bulls and bears will spin it to reinforce their priors.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Avoid over-indexing on prospectus details; the value depends on forward story assumptions, not historical disclosures.

insights.claim: Damodaran warns investors against AI-cabal conspiracy theories (hyper-scalers, chip makers and LLMs colluding to create a mirage) or presumptions of accounting fraud, saying self-interest and accounting discretion are common to all companies, not specific to AI or Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Bear cases built on fraud narratives are weak; focus critiques on fundamentals such as growth, margins and commitments.

themes.theme: Governance: share classes and PBC structure

insights.claim: Anthropic is going public with five share classes; Class A carries standard voting rights, but a benefit trust picks the board and founders control 50.1% of votes regardless of future issuance, which Damodaran says effectively emasculates public investors.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Public shareholders will have no path to force change; the only recourse is selling, which justifies a governance discount.

insights.claim: Anthropic's public benefit corporation status lets it make decisions that hurt business performance or the stock price; Damodaran argues this does not protect society from AI but concentrates power in the founders and benefit trust, calling it ESG-as-cover 'on steroids'.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Investors are legally subordinated to the Company Purpose; expect management decisions that sacrifice returns without recourse.
insights.quote: the Anthropic structure is that structure on steroids

insights.claim: Damodaran, who owns dual-class Alphabet and Meta, says Anthropic's combination of benefit-corporation status and its voting design puts those companies to shame, and that this structure requires a much larger discount to his value estimate before he would buy.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Value investors will demand a buy price well below $1.475 trillion intrinsic value, limiting fundamental demand at IPO pricing.
insights.locator: As an investor who holds shares

insights.claim: Damodaran argues governance scores have been gamed by companies and are poor indicators of shareholder power, and that institutional investors' passivity when Google issued dual-class shares at its IPO opened the door for tech founders to entrench control.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Ignore governance scores; judge governance by whether shareholders can actually force change.

insights.claim: Damodaran believes Anthropic's governance and lock-up terms dare institutional investors to protest by skipping the IPO, and that the company has calculated they will stay passive.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Expect a full book despite governance objections; institutional demand will not discipline the terms.
insights.locator: As you look at both the corporate governance

insights.claim: After nineteen funding rounds, Anthropic insiders (excluding founders and certain major figures) may sell up to 10% of their shares on the first trading day, the rest unlock in tranches over the first 180 days, and founders and key figures can sell after 365 days.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Supply hits the market from day one and in tranches through 180 days; mark the unlock calendar even if effects are muted.

insights.claim: Damodaran argues too much is made of share unlocks: with large institutional holders and ample liquidity the price effect at Anthropic will be muted, and 'smart money' selling at unlocks carries far less information than assumed.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Fading unlock-date shorts may work; insider selling should not be read as a strong bearish signal.
insights.locator: To be honest, I think that too much

insights.claim: Damodaran will sit out the Anthropic IPO if it prices well above his $1.48 trillion value, but will not short it because he has no reason to believe the market will correct within his time horizon.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Overvaluation is not a short signal for a hyped, liquid AI IPO; timing risk dominates.

insights.claim: Damodaran predicts there will almost certainly be a day when Anthropic is undervalued, possibly soon, citing Facebook, which he found overvalued at its $36 June 2012 IPO but bought three months later at $18.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Keep a watchlist entry with a target buy price below intrinsic value; post-IPO drawdowns in story stocks create entry points.
insights.quote: it is just as possible that major parts of the storyline, from revenue growth to margins to risk, will come under stress
